problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.statement:
Given a 1-indexed array of integers `numbers` that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific `target` number.

Return the indices of the two numbers, `index1` and `index2`, added by one as an integer array `[index1, index2]` of length 2.

You may not use the same element twice. Your solution must use only constant extra space.
constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order.
commonMistakes: Using 0-indexing instead of 1-indexing in return value
Using O(N) Hash Map space when problem requires O(1) space
hints: Since the array is sorted, can you use two converging pointers?
If numbers[left] + numbers[right] < target, increment left to increase sum.
If sum > target, decrement right to decrease sum.
Remember to return 1-based indices [left + 1, right + 1].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=5000 for complexity verification

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.statement:
Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, and `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

Notice that the solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.
commonMistakes: Failing to skip duplicate numbers for i, l, and r, creating duplicate triplets
Not sorting array first
hints: Sort the array first so you can use two pointers.
Fix the first number nums[i], then use two pointers on the remainder to find pairs summing to -nums[i].
Skip identical consecutive elements to avoid duplicate triplets.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification

problems.title: 3Sum Closest
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums` of length `n` and an integer `target`, find three integers in `nums` such that the sum is closest to `target`.

Return the sum of the three integers.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for 3Sum Closest testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Returning the absolute difference instead of the actual sum
hints: Sort the array and fix the first element nums[i].
Use two pointers (l, r) to find the closest pair sum.
Track the minimum difference |sum - target|.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=500 for complexity verification

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.statement:
Given an array `nums` of `n` integers, return an array of all the unique quadruplets `[nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]]` such that:
- `0 <= a, b, c, d < n`
- `a, b, c, and d` are distinct
- `nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] + nums[d] == target`

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for 4Sum testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: 32-bit integer overflow when adding 4 large 10^9 numbers in languages without 64-bit default
Duplicate quadruplets
hints: Sort nums first.
Fix the first two numbers (i, j), then use two pointers (l, r) for the remaining two.
Skip duplicates at all 4 levels.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. There are `n` vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the `i`th line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`.

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the most water.

Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

Notice that you may not slant the container.

examples.explanation: Lines at index 1 and 8 have heights 8 and 7, width 7 -> 7 * 7 = 49.
Edge/boundary case for Container With Most Water testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Moving the pointer with larger height (which can never increase the area since width shrinks and height is bottlenecked by the shorter bar)
hints: Start with pointers at both ends (maximum possible width).
The area is bounded by min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left).
To potentially find a larger area with smaller width, you MUST move the pointer pointing to the shorter vertical bar.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=5000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.statement: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Trapping Rain Water testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Failing to recognize that water trapped at i depends on min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height[i]
hints: Water at any bar is determined by min(max_left, max_right) - height[i].
Use two pointers from left and right maintaining leftMax and rightMax.
Always advance the pointer corresponding to the smaller maximum height.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=2000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove some duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears at most twice. The relative order of the elements should be kept the same.

Return `k` after placing the final result in the first `k` slots of `nums`.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Comparing nums[i] with nums[i-2] instead of nums[write-2]
hints: Generalize to at most K duplicates: allow nums[i] if nums[i] !== nums[write - K].
Here K = 2.
Advance write pointer only when a valid element is placed.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=2000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
problems.statement: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number sorted in non-decreasing order.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Squares of a Sorted Array testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Squaring each element and sorting O(N log N) instead of two pointers O(N)
hints: The largest square must be either at the far left (most negative) or far right (most positive).
Place two pointers at ends and fill the result array from right to left.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.statement:
Given an array `nums` with `n` objects colored red, white, or blue, sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent, with the colors in the order red, white, and blue.

We will use the integers `0`, `1`, and `2` to represent the color red, white, and blue, respectively.

You must solve this problem without using the library's sort function in one pass and using only constant extra space.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Sort Colors testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Advancing mid pointer after swapping with high (element swapped from high is unexamined)
hints: Use the Dutch National Flag 3-way partitioning algorithm.
Maintain three pointers: low, mid, and high.
When swapping with high, do NOT increment mid because the newly swapped value has not been evaluated.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification

problems.title: Reverse Vowels of a String
problems.statement:
Given a string `s`, reverse only all the vowels in the string and return it.

The vowels are 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', and 'u', and they can appear in both lower and upper cases, more than once.
constraints: s consist of printable ASCII characters.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Reverse Vowels of a String testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Missing uppercase vowels ('A', 'E', 'I', 'O', 'U')
hints: Include both lowercase and uppercase vowels.
Use two pointers from left and right converging towards the center.
Swap vowels when both pointers land on vowels.

problems.title: Backspace String Compare
problems.statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if they are equal when both are typed into empty text editors. `'#'` means a backspace character.

Note that after backspacing an empty text, the text will continue to be empty.

Can you solve it in `O(N)` time and `O(1)` space?
constraints: s and t only contain lowercase letters and '#' characters.
commonMistakes: Simulating forwards which requires stack (O(N) space) instead of backwards O(1) space
hints: Iterate backwards from the end of both strings.
Count '#' characters to know how many upcoming letters to skip.
Compare characters when both strings have an active, non-backspaced character.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=200 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=150 for complexity verification

problems.title: Is Subsequence
problems.statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `s` is a subsequence of `t`, or `false` otherwise.

A subsequence of a string is a new string that is formed from the original string by deleting some (can be none) of the characters without disturbing the relative positions of the remaining characters.
constraints: s and t consist only of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Is Subsequence testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Empty string s edge case (empty string is always a subsequence)
hints: Maintain a pointer i for s and pointer j for t.
Advance i whenever s[i] matches t[j]. Always advance j.
If i reaches s.length, all characters were found in order.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification

problems.title: Two Sum Less Than K
problems.statement: Given an array `nums` of integers and integer `k`, return the maximum sum `nums[i] + nums[j]` such that `i < j` and `nums[i] + nums[j] < k`. If no such `i, j` exist, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Two Sum Less Than K testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Allowing sum === k (problem states strictly less than k)
hints: Sort nums in ascending order.
Use two pointers at opposite ends.
If sum < k, record it and increment left; otherwise decrement right.

problems.title: Boats to Save People
problems.statement:
You are given an array `people` where `people[i]` is the weight of the `i`th person, and an infinite number of boats where each boat can carry a maximum weight of `limit`.

Each boat carries at most two people at the same time, provided the sum of the weight of those people is at most `limit`.

Return the minimum number of boats to carry every given person.
commonMistakes: Trying to put more than 2 people in one boat (limit is at most 2 people)
hints: Sort people by weight.
Greedily pair the heaviest person with the lightest person if their combined weight <= limit.
The heaviest person always takes a boat.

Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Interval List Intersections
problems.statement:
You are given two lists of closed intervals, `firstList` and `secondList`, where `firstList[i] = [starti, endi]` and `secondList[j] = [startj, endj]`.

Return the intersection of these two interval lists.

A closed interval `[a, b]` (with `a <= b`) denotes the set of real numbers `x` with `a <= x <= b`.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Interval List Intersections testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Advancing the interval with smaller start instead of smaller END
hints: Overlap between [s1, e1] and [s2, e2] is [max(s1, s2), min(e1, e2)] if max <= min.
Discard the interval that finishes earlier (smaller end value) because it cannot intersect any future interval.

problems.title: Partition Labels
problems.statement:
You are given a string `s`. We want to partition the string into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part.

Note that the partition is done so that after concatenating all the parts in order, the resultant string should be `s`.

Return a list of integers representing the size of these parts.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Partition Labels testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Splitting partition before reaching the last occurrence of all letters inside it
hints: Precompute the last index where each character appears.
As you iterate, expand the current partition's end to max(end, last[s[i]]).
When i reaches end, a valid partition boundary is found.

problems.title: String Compression
problems.statement:
Given an array of characters `chars`, compress it using the following algorithm:

Begin with an empty string `s`. For each group of consecutive repeating characters in `chars`:
- If group length is 1, append the character to `s`.
- Otherwise, append the character followed by the group's length.

Return the new length of the array after in-place modification.
constraints: chars[i] is a lowercase English letter, uppercase letter, digit, or symbol.
commonMistakes: Multi-digit counts: count 12 must be written as '1' and '2' across two slots
hints: Use read and write pointers.
Count length of each contiguous character block.
If count > 1, convert to string and write each digit into chars[write++].

Stress test scale N=2000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Next Permutation
problems.statement:
A permutation of an array of integers is an arrangement of its members into a sequence or linear order.

Given an array of integers `nums`, find the next lexicographical permutation of its elements.

If such an arrangement is not possible, the array must be rearranged as the lowest possible order (i.e., sorted in ascending order).

The replacement must be in place and use only constant extra memory.
commonMistakes: Failing to reverse the suffix after swapping (suffix is descending, so reversing it makes it ascending in O(N))
hints: Find the first decreasing element nums[i] from right to left.
Find the element nums[j] to the right of i that is strictly greater than nums[i].
Swap nums[i] and nums[j], then reverse the suffix from i + 1 to the end.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification

problems.title: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, you need to find one continuous subarray that if you only sort this subarray in ascending order, then the whole array will be sorted in ascending order.

Return the shortest such subarray and output its length.
commonMistakes: Sorting the array which takes O(N log N) time and O(N) space
hints: The right boundary is the last element smaller than the running maximum from the left.
The left boundary is the last element greater than the running minimum from the right.
Both boundaries can be found simultaneously in a single pass.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Valid Triangle Number
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of triplets chosen from the array that can make triangles if we take them as side lengths of a triangle.

Three side lengths `a, b, c` form a valid triangle if `a + b > c`, `a + c > b`, and `b + c > a`.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Valid Triangle Number testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Zero side lengths cannot form a triangle
Missing the property that if sorted, nums[l] + nums[r] > nums[k] means all indices from l to r-1 also satisfy it with r
hints: Sort the array ascending.
Fix the longest side nums[k] starting from the end.
If nums[l] + nums[r] > nums[k], then every index between l and r-1 will also satisfy the triangle inequality with nums[r], adding r - l pairs at once.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification

problems.title: 3Sum With Multiplicity
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `arr`, and an integer `target`, return the number of tuples `i, j, k` such that `i < j < k` and `arr[i] + arr[j] + arr[k] == target`.

As the answer can be very large, return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for 3Sum With Multiplicity testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Combinatorics edge cases when all 3 numbers are equal vs 2 numbers equal
hints: Notice the values in arr are bounded between 0 and 100.
Count the frequency of each number from 0 to 100.
Iterate over unique pairs (i, j) where i <= j and k = target - i - j >= j.
Use combinations formulas nC3 and nC2.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1500 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=2000 for complexity verification
